To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) losses improve cognitive performance, (2) this effect is stronger when the loss is more salient (e.g., because it is larger), (3) this effect is weaker when a disadvantageous option produces the loss, (4) losses improve cognitive task performance even when the contrast effect is absent (i.e., when a similar loss is attached to all options), and (5) these effects cannot be accounted for by the theory of loss aversion.
losses improve performance even if they are not more salient than gains, and even when losses are not weighted more than gains.
losses improve performance in the absence of loss aversion, and the effects are driven by attention and/or contrast effects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of losses on cognitive functioning.
the impact of loss on decision-making and performance.

the impact of incentives on cognitive performance and shows that losses have positive effects on performance, which are mediated by two different mechanisms: attention to task incentives and contrast effects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of losses is a combination of the two processes: attention to losses and the effect of contrast.
the effect of losses is due to a combination of attentional processes and contrast effects, which may or may not be accompanied by loss aversion.
loss aversion is one mechanism that can account for the positive effect of losses, but that it is not the only one.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
losses improve cognitive performance by drawing attention and by increasing sensitivity to task incentives.
losses can improve performance, but the effect is not due to loss aversion.
losses improve performance, and this effect is driven by a joint effect of increased attention and contrast-related processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of losses is not always loss aversion.
losses can have positive effects on performance, and the effect of losses is not necessarily a reflection of loss aversion, but rather can be explained by the attentional effects of losses.
